questions.title: Triclabendazole is the drug of choice for treatment of infection by:
questions.question: Triclabendazole is the drug of choice for treatment of infection by:

explanations.A: Taenia solium is a cestode, not the fluke this triclabendazole question concerns, and it is treated with praziquantel, not triclabendazole.
explanations.B: Taenia saginata is a cestode treated with praziquantel; triclabendazole is not indicated for it.
explanations.C: Hymenolepis nana is a cestode treated with praziquantel; triclabendazole is not indicated for it.
explanations.D: Triclabendazole is the drug of choice for Fasciola hepatica infection, because the adult and migrating immature fluke are both susceptible to its mechanism, unlike the case with praziquantel, which is ineffective against Fasciola despite being broadly active against most other trematodes and cestodes. This drug-species pairing is a standard, frequently tested exception in medical parasitology: praziquantel covers almost everything except Fasciola, and triclabendazole is the specific answer whenever a Fasciola treatment question is asked. Recognising Fasciola as the exception to praziquantel's broad spectrum is exactly the fact this question is testing.

questions.title: Praziquantel is the drug of choice in treatment of infection of:
questions.question: Praziquantel is the drug of choice in treatment of infection of:

explanations.A: Praziquantel genuinely is the drug of choice for Taenia solium, so this option alone is true but incomplete.
explanations.B: Praziquantel genuinely is the drug of choice for Heterophyes heterophyes, so this option alone is true but incomplete.
explanations.C: Praziquantel genuinely is the drug of choice for Hymenolepis nana, so this option alone is true but incomplete.
explanations.D: Praziquantel is the drug of choice for all three infections listed — Taenia solium, Heterophyes heterophyes and Hymenolepis nana — reflecting its broad activity across cestodes and most trematodes by increasing the parasite tegument's calcium permeability, causing spastic paralysis and detachment from the gut wall. This wide spectrum is why praziquantel is the default anthelmintic reached for across the cestode and trematode infections in this cluster, with Fasciola as the standing exception. Recognising that all three named organisms share praziquantel as their drug of choice, rather than any one of them being an exception, is the point of this question.

questions.title: The snail which resists molluscicidal agent is:
questions.question: The snail which resists molluscicidal agent is:

explanations.A: Bulinus truncatus is the fresh-water intermediate host snail for Schistosoma haematobium and is susceptible to standard molluscicides, not the resistant snail this question asks about.
explanations.B: Pirenella conica, the brackish-water snail that transmits Heterophyes heterophyes, is resistant to the molluscicidal agents that are effective against the fresh-water snails used to transmit schistosomiasis. Its brackish habitat and physiological differences from fresh-water snails such as Bulinus truncatus and Biomphalaria alexandrina make standard control programmes ineffective against it. This resistance is a recognised obstacle to controlling heterophyiasis transmission and is the specific fact this question tests.
explanations.C: Biomphalaria alexandrina is the fresh-water intermediate host snail for Schistosoma mansoni and is susceptible to standard molluscicides, not the resistant snail this question asks about.
explanations.D: Lymnaea caillaudi is a fresh-water snail that transmits Fasciola gigantica and is susceptible to standard molluscicides, not the resistant snail this question asks about.

questions.title: The snail which lives in brackish water is:
questions.question: The snail which lives in brackish water is:

explanations.A: Bulinus truncatus lives in fresh water, transmitting Schistosoma haematobium, not the brackish-water snail this question asks about.
explanations.B: Pirenella conica is the snail that lives in brackish water, the mixed salt-and-fresh water typical of estuaries and coastal lagoons, and it serves as the intermediate host for Heterophyes heterophyes. This brackish habitat distinguishes it sharply from the fresh-water snails, Bulinus truncatus, Biomphalaria alexandrina and Lymnaea species, that transmit schistosomiasis and fascioliasis. Its habitat is directly linked to Heterophyes heterophyes's distribution along brackish coastal waters and irrigation canals with saline intrusion.
explanations.C: Biomphalaria alexandrina lives in fresh water, transmitting Schistosoma mansoni, not the brackish-water snail this question asks about.
explanations.D: Lymnaea caillaudi lives in fresh water, transmitting Fasciola gigantica, not the brackish-water snail this question asks about.

questions.title: Leptocercus cercaria emerges from the following snail:
questions.question: Leptocercus cercaria emerges from the following snail:

explanations.A: Lymnaea truncatula does shed leptocercous cercariae (for Fasciola hepatica), but it is not the only correct answer among these options.
explanations.B: The planorbid Segmentina snail does shed leptocercous cercariae (for Fasciolopsis buski), but it is not the only correct answer among these options.
explanations.C: Lymnaea caillaudi does shed leptocercous cercariae (for Fasciola gigantica), but it is not the only correct answer among these options.
explanations.D: Leptocercous (long-tailed) cercariae emerge from all three snails listed: Lymnaea truncatula, which produces the cercariae of Fasciola hepatica; Lymnaea caillaudi, which produces those of Fasciola gigantica; and the planorbid Segmentina snail, which produces those of Fasciolopsis buski. All three of these large flukes share the same leptocercous cercarial body plan, in contrast to the lophocercous cercaria produced by Pirenella conica for Heterophyes heterophyes. Recognising that leptocercous morphology spans multiple snail hosts and flukes, rather than being tied to just one, is what this question tests.

questions.title: Lophocercus cercaria emerges from the following snail:
questions.question: Lophocercus cercaria emerges from the following snail:

explanations.A: Lymnaea truncatula sheds leptocercous, not lophocercous, cercariae, developing into Fasciola hepatica.
explanations.B: The Segmentina snail sheds leptocercous, not lophocercous, cercariae, developing into Fasciolopsis buski.
explanations.C: Pirenella conica is the snail that sheds the lophocercous (finned-tail) cercaria, which develops into the intestinal fluke Heterophyes heterophyes. This pairing distinguishes Pirenella conica's brackish-water lophocercous cercaria from the leptocercous cercariae shed by the fresh-water Lymnaea and Segmentina snails that produce Fasciola and Fasciolopsis buski respectively. Matching lophocercous cercarial morphology specifically to Pirenella conica is the fact tested here.
explanations.D: Lymnaea caillaudi sheds leptocercous, not lophocercous, cercariae, developing into Fasciola gigantica.

questions.title: Lophocercus cercaria is a stage in the life cycle of the following parasite:
questions.question: Lophocercus cercaria is a stage in the life cycle of the following parasite:

explanations.A: The lophocercous cercaria, shed by Pirenella conica, develops into the adult fluke Heterophyes heterophyes, the small intestinal fluke acquired by eating undercooked brackish-water fish carrying its encysted metacercaria. This finned-tail cercarial morphology is characteristic of Heterophyes among the flukes in this cluster, distinguishing its life cycle stage from the leptocercous cercariae of Fasciola and Fasciolopsis buski. Recognising the lophocercous cercaria as specifically a Heterophyes heterophyes life-cycle stage is the point of this question.
explanations.B: Fasciola hepatica develops from a leptocercous, not lophocercous, cercaria shed by Lymnaea truncatula.
explanations.C: Fasciola gigantica develops from a leptocercous, not lophocercous, cercaria shed by Lymnaea caillaudi.
explanations.D: Fasciolopsis buski develops from a leptocercous, not lophocercous, cercaria shed by the Segmentina snail.

questions.title: As regards halzoon, all are true except:
questions.question: As regards halzoon, all are true except:

options.B: Encysted metacercariae are attached to the pharynx
options.C: It is caused by eating raw livers of infected sheep and cattle
options.D: It is treated by gargling with alcoholic drink

explanations.A: Halzoon genuinely is the pharyngeal form of fascioliasis, so this true statement is not the exception.
explanations.B: It is the adult Fasciola worm, released alive from raw infected liver, that attaches to the pharyngeal or laryngeal mucosa in halzoon, not the encysted metacercaria, which is the infective stage acquired from contaminated vegetation in ordinary fascioliasis, an entirely different route. This is the false statement among the four, which is why it is the exception the question asks for. The other three statements correctly describe halzoon's cause (eating raw infected liver), source animals (sheep and cattle) and treatment (astringent gargle).
explanations.C: Halzoon genuinely is caused by eating raw livers of infected sheep and cattle still harbouring live adult worms, so this true statement is not the exception.
explanations.D: Halzoon genuinely is treated by gargling with an alcoholic drink, which acts as an astringent to detach the attached worms, so this true statement is not the exception.

questions.title: As regards fascioliasis, all are true except:
questions.question: As regards fascioliasis, all are true except:

options.A: Infection is by eating contaminated vegetables
options.C: Praziquantel is the drug of choice
options.D: The acute phase of the disease begins 2 months after infection

explanations.A: Fascioliasis genuinely is acquired by eating contaminated vegetables carrying encysted metacercariae, so this true statement is not the exception.
explanations.B: The encysted metacercaria genuinely is the infective stage of fascioliasis, so this true statement is not the exception.
explanations.C: Praziquantel is not the drug of choice for fascioliasis; Fasciola is specifically resistant to it, and triclabendazole is the correct drug of choice instead. This is the false statement among the four, which is why it is the exception the question asks for. The other three statements correctly describe the vegetable-borne route, the metacercarial infective stage, and the roughly two-month onset of the acute hepatic phase.
explanations.D: The acute phase of fascioliasis genuinely does begin around two months after infection, reflecting the time the immature flukes take to migrate through the liver parenchyma, so this true statement is not the exception.

questions.title: False fascioliasis may result from:
questions.question: False fascioliasis may result from:

options.A: Ingestion of infected liver with dead Fasciola adults
options.D: Ingestion of encysted metacercariae in vegetables

explanations.A: False fascioliasis results from eating liver from an infected animal that still contains dead adult Fasciola worms or their unabsorbed eggs, which then pass through the human digestive tract and appear in stool without ever establishing a true infection in the person's own bile ducts. This distinguishes false fascioliasis from genuine infection, where a live adult worm becomes established after ingesting encysted metacercariae from contaminated vegetation. Recognising the liver-meal route as the cause of false, rather than true, fascioliasis is the point of this question.
explanations.B: Insufficiently cooked meat is not the transmission route of fascioliasis, whether true or false; it is a route for cestode infections such as taeniasis, not for Fasciola.
explanations.C: Drinking infected water is not the standard transmission route for fascioliasis; the metacercaria encysts on aquatic vegetation, not free in water.
explanations.D: Ingesting encysted metacercariae on vegetables produces true fascioliasis with an established adult worm, not the false (spurious) pattern this question asks about.

questions.title: As regards fascioliasis, the false answer is:
questions.question: As regards fascioliasis, the false answer is:

options.A: It presents by fever, hepatomegaly, anemia and eosinophilia
options.D: Infective stage is encysted metacercaria in fish

explanations.A: Fascioliasis genuinely does present with fever, hepatomegaly, anemia and eosinophilia during its hepatic migratory phase, so this true statement is not the false answer.
explanations.B: Duodenal aspiration genuinely can reveal Fasciola eggs once the flukes have matured in the bile ducts, since bile drains into the duodenum, so this true statement is not the false answer.
explanations.C: Fascioliasis genuinely is treated by triclabendazole, so this true statement is not the false answer.
explanations.D: The infective stage of fascioliasis, the encysted metacercaria, is found on aquatic vegetation such as watercress, not in fish, which is why this is the false statement among the four. Metacercariae in fish instead characterise Heterophyes heterophyes and Diphyllobothrium latum's life cycles, a different transmission pattern from Fasciola's vegetable-borne route. Distinguishing Fasciola's vegetation-based metacercarial source from the fish-based source of other GIT-301 helminths is the fact this question tests.

questions.title: For early diagnosis and detection of Fasciola gigantica infection, the best investigation is:
questions.question: For early diagnosis and detection of Fasciola gigantica infection, the best investigation is:

options.A: Stool examination to detect the eggs

explanations.A: Stool examination for eggs is unreliable for early diagnosis, because the migrating immature fluke has not yet reached the bile ducts and begun laying eggs during the pre-patent period.
explanations.B: For early diagnosis of Fasciola gigantica infection, indirect serological testing (ELISA) is the best investigation, because it detects the host's antibody response to migrating larvae well before the fluke reaches patency and begins shedding eggs into stool, which can take several months. This makes serology far more sensitive than stool-based methods during the acute, pre-patent phase of the disease. Recognising that early diagnosis depends on antibody detection rather than egg detection is the point of this question.
explanations.C: Demonstrating copro-antigen in stool still depends on the fluke being established and shedding antigen into the gut, making it, like egg detection, less useful very early in infection than serology.
explanations.D: Liver function tests can show nonspecific abnormalities during hepatic migration but are not a specific diagnostic test for early Fasciola gigantica infection.

questions.title: Spurious infection occurs in:
questions.question: Spurious infection occurs in:

explanations.A: Spurious infection occurs in Fasciola gigantica, in which eggs or dead worms from an ingested infected liver pass through the human gut and appear transiently in stool, without the patient having a true established infection in their own bile ducts. This phenomenon is the same false/spurious fascioliasis pattern tested elsewhere in this cluster, and Fasciola gigantica is the species classically cited for it. Recognising that spurious passage, rather than genuine parasitism, explains these stool findings is the point of this question.
explanations.B: Diphyllobothrium latum, the fish tapeworm, is not classically associated with spurious infection from liver ingestion; its eggs are diagnosed from a true established intestinal infection.
explanations.C: Metagonimus yokogawi is a fish-borne intestinal fluke not classically associated with spurious infection from eating liver.
explanations.D: Clonorchis sinensis is a liver fluke acquired from fish, not classically associated with spurious infection from eating liver.

questions.title: In pharyngeal fascioliasis (halzoon), the parasitic stage that causes suffocation is:
questions.question: In pharyngeal fascioliasis (halzoon), the parasitic stage that causes suffocation is:

explanations.A: In pharyngeal fascioliasis (halzoon), it is the adult worm, released alive when raw infected liver is eaten, that attaches to the pharyngeal or laryngeal mucosa and causes the oedema and swelling that can lead to suffocation. This is distinct from ordinary fascioliasis, where the encysted metacercaria on vegetation is the infective stage that establishes true intestinal-to-hepatic infection. Identifying the adult worm, not an egg, cercaria or metacercaria, as the stage responsible for halzoon's suffocation risk is the fact tested here.
explanations.B: The egg is not the stage responsible for halzoon; eggs are shed by the established adult worm in the bile ducts, not released from ingested raw liver to attach to the pharynx.
explanations.C: The cercaria is a free-swimming larval stage that emerges from the snail intermediate host in water, not the stage responsible for pharyngeal attachment after eating raw liver.
explanations.D: The encysted metacercaria is the infective stage acquired from contaminated vegetation in ordinary fascioliasis, not the stage that causes halzoon after eating raw infected liver.

questions.title: Operculated eggs containing immature embryo in Trematoda are diagnostic stages in stool except:
questions.question: Operculated eggs containing immature embryo in Trematoda are diagnostic stages in stool except:

explanations.A: Heterophyes heterophyes is the exception among these trematode eggs: its egg is already embryonated, containing a fully developed miracidium, when it is laid, rather than being immature like the eggs of Fasciolopsis buski, Fasciola hepatica and Fasciola gigantica. This is why it is the answer to this "except" question about immature operculated eggs. Heterophyes's small embryonated egg must instead be ingested directly by its snail host, Pirenella conica, to complete hatching.
explanations.B: Fasciolopsis buski genuinely lays an immature operculated egg, so this true statement is not the exception.
explanations.C: Fasciola hepatica genuinely lays an immature operculated egg, so this true statement is not the exception.
explanations.D: Fasciola gigantica genuinely lays an immature operculated egg, so this true statement is not the exception.

questions.title: Adult worms of the following Trematoda lay immature operculated eggs except:
questions.question: Adult worms of the following Trematoda lay immature operculated eggs except:

explanations.A: Heterophyes heterophyes is the exception: its adult worms lay eggs that are already embryonated with a developed miracidium at the time of laying, unlike Fasciolopsis buski, Fasciola hepatica and Fasciola gigantica, which all lay immature operculated eggs that develop further after being passed. This embryonated-at-laying pattern is directly linked to Heterophyes's unusual requirement that its egg be ingested by the snail host rather than hatching freely. This is why Heterophyes heterophyes is the correct answer to this "except" question.
explanations.B: Fasciolopsis buski adults genuinely lay immature operculated eggs, so this true statement is not the exception.
explanations.C: Fasciola hepatica adults genuinely lay immature operculated eggs, so this true statement is not the exception.
explanations.D: Fasciola gigantica adults genuinely lay immature operculated eggs, so this true statement is not the exception.

questions.title: All the Trematoda eggs hatch in water to give miracidium, except:
questions.question: All the Trematoda eggs hatch in water to give miracidium, except:

explanations.A: Heterophyes heterophyes is the exception: its egg does not hatch freely in water at all, because it is already embryonated when laid and must instead be ingested directly by the Pirenella conica snail, inside which hatching then occurs. Fasciola gigantica, Fasciolopsis buski and Fasciola hepatica, by contrast, all lay immature eggs that hatch in water to release a free-swimming miracidium once conditions are suitable. This water-hatching exception is the specific fact tested here.
explanations.B: Fasciola gigantica eggs genuinely hatch in water to release a miracidium, so this true statement is not the exception.
explanations.C: Fasciolopsis buski eggs genuinely hatch in water to release a miracidium, so this true statement is not the exception.
explanations.D: Fasciola hepatica eggs genuinely hatch in water to release a miracidium, so this true statement is not the exception.

questions.title: In human liver, Fasciola worms reside in:
questions.question: In human liver, Fasciola worms reside in:

explanations.A: Fasciola worms migrate through liver cells during the acute invasive phase but do not reside there once mature; the parenchymal phase is transient, not their final habitat.
explanations.B: Portal blood vessels are not where mature Fasciola worms reside; the immature fluke migrates through the peritoneal cavity and liver parenchyma before reaching the bile ducts, not the portal venous system.
explanations.C: Liver sinusoids are traversed during larval migration but are not the site where the mature Fasciola worm settles.
explanations.D: In the human liver, mature Fasciola worms reside in the bile ducts, having migrated there from the peritoneal cavity through the liver capsule and parenchyma during the acute phase of infection. This biliary habitat is where the worms feed on blood and biliary epithelium and shed eggs that pass into the duodenum with bile, and it is also why chronic fascioliasis can cause biliary obstruction and secondary cholangitis. Knowing the bile duct as the adult worm's final habitat, distinct from the parenchymal route it took to get there, is the fact tested here.

questions.title: Vitamin B12 deficiency anemia may occur in infection with:
questions.question: Vitamin B12 deficiency anemia may occur in infection with:

explanations.A: Heterophyes heterophyes is not linked to B12 deficiency anemia in this bank's key; its recognised complications are ectopic egg embolism and myocarditis instead.
explanations.B: Fasciola gigantica is not linked to B12 deficiency anemia in this bank's key; its recognised complications relate to hepatobiliary disease from bile duct infestation.
explanations.C: Vitamin B12 deficiency anemia may occur in infection with Fasciolopsis buski, per this bank's printed key, attributed to the malabsorption syndrome that heavy infection produces by damaging the duodenal and jejunal mucosa where the giant intestinal fluke attaches. The more classically taught mechanism for helminth-associated B12 deficiency, direct competitive uptake of the vitamin by the worm itself, is instead usually attributed to Diphyllobothrium latum, the fish tapeworm; this bank's key names Fasciolopsis buski instead, and it is kept as printed. Recognising the printed key's pairing, even where it differs from the most commonly taught example, is what this question, as printed, tests.
explanations.D: Fasciola hepatica is not linked to B12 deficiency anemia in this bank's key; its recognised complications relate to hepatobiliary disease from bile duct infestation.

questions.title: Egg emboli may occur in infection with:
questions.question: Egg emboli may occur in infection with:

explanations.A: Egg emboli may occur in infection with Heterophyes heterophyes, because some of its eggs penetrate the intestinal mucosa, enter mesenteric venules, and embolize through the venous and then arterial circulation to ectopic sites, most seriously the heart and central nervous system. This ectopic-embolization complication is unusual for what is otherwise a mild intestinal fluke infection, and it is why Heterophyes carries a recognised, if uncommon, risk of serious cardiac and neurological disease. Recognising Heterophyes heterophyes as the fluke whose eggs specifically embolize is the fact this question tests.
explanations.B: Fasciola gigantica causes hepatobiliary disease from bile duct infestation, not egg embolism to ectopic sites.
explanations.C: Fasciolopsis buski is confined to the intestinal lumen and does not cause egg embolism to ectopic sites.
explanations.D: Fasciola hepatica causes hepatobiliary disease from bile duct infestation, not egg embolism to ectopic sites.

questions.question: Infective stage of Diphyllobothrium latum is:

explanations.A: Plerocercoid in Cyclops is incorrect; Cyclops (a copepod) is the first intermediate host, harbouring the earlier, non-infective procercoid stage, not the plerocercoid.

questions.question: We can differentiate between Taenia solium and Taenia saginata infections by:

options.B: Staining their eggs by modified Ziehl-Neelsen
options.C: The morphology of their scolices in stool after successful treatment

explanations.A: Gravid segment morphology genuinely is one way to differentiate Taenia solium from Taenia saginata, so this option alone is true but incomplete.
explanations.B: Staining eggs with modified Ziehl-Neelsen genuinely is one described method for differentiating the two species' eggs, so this option alone is true but incomplete.
explanations.C: Examining the scolex recovered in stool after successful treatment genuinely is one way to differentiate the two species, so this option alone is true but incomplete.
explanations.D: Taenia solium and Taenia saginata can be differentiated by all three methods listed: the morphology of their gravid segments (including the lateral uterine branch count), modified Ziehl-Neelsen staining of their eggs, and the appearance of the scolex once recovered after successful treatment. Using multiple, mutually supporting methods, rather than relying on just one, is standard practice for confidently distinguishing these two closely related tapeworm species. Recognising that all three methods are simultaneously valid is what this question tests.

questions.title: Taenia solium is more dangerous than Taenia saginata due to:
questions.question: Taenia solium is more dangerous than Taenia saginata due to:

options.A: Autoinfection in T. solium leading to cysticercosis
options.B: The hooks in Taenia solium scolex leading to bleeding

explanations.A: Taenia solium is more dangerous than Taenia saginata because autoinfection is possible: a patient carrying the adult worm can ingest their own eggs, whether by faecal-oral contamination or reverse peristalsis, and those eggs can hatch and develop into cysticerci within the patient's own tissues, including the brain (neurocysticercosis). Taenia saginata carries no equivalent risk, because the human intestine is a dead end for its eggs, which can only develop into cysticerci after being ingested by cattle. This autoinfection-driven cysticercosis risk is the specific danger that sets T. solium apart and is the fact tested here.
explanations.B: The hooks on the Taenia solium scolex anchor the worm to the intestinal mucosa but are not the mechanism that makes the species more dangerous; that danger comes from the autoinfection/cysticercosis risk instead.
explanations.C: Only the autoinfection/cysticercosis mechanism, not the scolex hooks, correctly explains why Taenia solium is more dangerous, so "all the above" overstates the case.
explanations.D: A real, specific mechanism — autoinfection leading to cysticercosis — does explain Taenia solium's added danger, so "none of all" is incorrect.

questions.question: Vitamin B12 deficiency anemia in Cestoda may be caused by:

explanations.A: Vitamin B12 deficiency anemia in Cestoda may be caused by Diphyllobothrium latum, the fish tapeworm, which competes directly with its host for dietary vitamin B12 absorbed in the small intestine, producing a megaloblastic anemia in heavily infected patients. questions.question: Alveolar hydatid cyst is commonly found in:

explanations.A: Alveolar hydatid cyst, caused by the larval stage of Echinococcus multilocularis, is commonly found in the liver, in 90 to 100% of cases, reflecting the portal venous route by which the oncosphere reaches the liver after being ingested and hatching in the intestine. The mass grows diffusely and infiltratively within the liver, in a pattern that behaves much like a malignant tumour.

explanations.C: The brain is a rare site for alveolar hydatid disease, far less common than the liver.
explanations.D: Bone is a rare site for alveolar hydatid disease, far less common than the liver.

explanations.A: The intermediate hosts of the alveolar hydatid cyst (Echinococcus multilocularis) are rodents, with man an occasional, accidental intermediate host who becomes infected by ingesting eggs shed by the definitive host, typically a fox. questions.question: The drug of choice for treatment of Taenia solium infection is:

explanations.A: Yomesan (niclosamide) is an effective alternative anticestode drug for taeniasis, but it is not the drug of choice ahead of praziquantel.
explanations.B: Metrifonate is an antischistosomal drug and has no role in treating Taenia solium infection.

questions.title: Man can act as blind intermediate host in infection with:
questions.question: Man can act as blind intermediate host in infection with:

explanations.A: Hymenolepis diminuta requires an arthropod intermediate host, not man, and man does not typically act as its intermediate host.
explanations.B: Taenia saginata uses man as its definitive host and cattle as its intermediate host; man does not act as an intermediate host for T. saginata.
explanations.C: Man can act as a blind (accidental, dead-end) intermediate host in infection with Echinococcus granulosus, developing hydatid cysts, most often in the liver, after ingesting eggs shed by an infected dog, the normal definitive host. Recognising E. granulosus, rather than the tapeworms in the other options, as the species for which man is an accidental intermediate host is the fact tested here.
explanations.D: Hymenolepis nana completes its cycle directly within a single host and does not require man to serve as a distinct intermediate host in the way this question describes.

questions.title: Autoinfection is a mode of transmission of the following parasites:
questions.question: Autoinfection is a mode of transmission of the following parasites:

explanations.A: Taenia saginata cannot autoinfect its human host, since its eggs are only infective after developing into a cysticercus in cattle, the intermediate host.
explanations.B: Autoinfection is a recognised mode of transmission for Hymenolepis nana, because its direct life cycle allows eggs released by the adult worm in the intestine to re-infect the same host without ever leaving the body, hatching and developing through the cysticercoid stage in the intestinal villi again. This capacity for self-perpetuating infection is a major reason H. nana can produce heavy, persistent worm burdens, particularly in children in crowded or poor-hygiene settings. Recognising H. nana as capable of autoinfection, unlike the intermediate-host-dependent tapeworms, is the point of this question.
explanations.C: Echinococcus granulosus requires a dog definitive host and a separate intermediate host (commonly sheep) and does not autoinfect a single human host.
explanations.D: Only Hymenolepis nana, not "all of the above," is capable of this direct-cycle autoinfection among the options listed.

questions.question: The larval stage of the following parasite has a malignant-like behaviour in human tissue:

explanations.A: Taenia saginata's larval stage (Cysticercus bovis) develops within discrete, encapsulated cysts in cattle muscle and does not show malignant-like infiltrative behaviour.
explanations.B: The larval stage of alveolar hydatid disease (Echinococcus multilocularis) has a malignant-like behaviour in human tissue, infiltrating and destroying surrounding tissue diffusely rather than remaining confined within a well-defined capsule, in contrast to the discretely encapsulated cystic (unilocular) hydatid of Echinococcus granulosus. This locally invasive, tumour-like growth pattern is what makes alveolar hydatid disease more dangerous and harder to manage than cystic hydatid disease, sometimes requiring management approaches that resemble those for malignancy. Recognising alveolar hydatid disease as the option with this malignant-like behaviour is the fact tested here.
explanations.C: Echinococcus granulosus's hydatid cyst is a well-encapsulated, discrete cystic lesion, not one with malignant-like infiltrative behaviour.
explanations.D: Hymenolepis diminuta's larval stage (cysticercoid) develops within an arthropod intermediate host and is not associated with malignant-like tissue infiltration in man.

questions.question: The following parasite is the commonest cestode affecting children:

explanations.A: Hymenolepis nana is the commonest cestode affecting children, favoured by its ability to spread directly from person to person and by autoinfection, both of which promote heavy transmission in crowded settings such as schools and households with poor hygiene. Recognising H. nana, rather than Echinococcus granulosus or either Taenia species, as the commonest childhood cestode is the fact tested here.
explanations.B: Echinococcus granulosus, causing hydatid disease, is not the commonest cestode of childhood; its acquisition depends on dog-sheep-human cycles rather than the person-to-person spread that makes H. nana so common in children.
explanations.C: Taenia solium is acquired from undercooked pork and is not the commonest cestode of childhood.
explanations.D: Taenia saginata is acquired from undercooked beef and is not the commonest cestode of childhood.

questions.question: The gravid proglottid of Taenia saginata can be best differentiated from that of Taenia solium by the:

options.A: Morphology of the ova within uterus
options.B: Number of ova within the uterus

explanations.A: The morphology of ova within the uterus is not the most reliable differentiating feature between the two species' gravid proglottids; the branch count is.
explanations.B: The number of ova within the uterus is not the standard differentiating feature used; the number of branching points (lateral uterine branches) is what is counted.

This branch-counting method is the single most reliable morphological way to distinguish the two species' gravid segments when the scolex is not available for examination. Recognising uterine branch count, rather than ovum morphology, number or segment colour, as the key differentiating feature is the fact tested here.

questions.question: The 2nd intermediate host of Diphyllobothrium latum:

questions.question: The larval stage of Hymenolepis nana is:

questions.question: To complete the life cycle, Hymenolepis diminuta eggs must be ingested by:

explanations.A: To complete its life cycle, Hymenolepis diminuta eggs must be ingested by a suitable arthropod intermediate host, such as a grain beetle or flea, within which the egg develops into a cysticercoid larva; the definitive host (typically a rodent, occasionally man) is then infected by accidentally ingesting the infected arthropod, for example in contaminated stored grain. This obligate arthropod-intermediate-host requirement distinguishes H. diminuta's life cycle from the direct, no-intermediate-host cycle of Hymenolepis nana. Recognising the arthropod as the required intermediate host for H. diminuta is the fact tested here.
explanations.B: A dog is not the required intermediate host for Hymenolepis diminuta; its cycle depends on an arthropod intermediate host instead.
explanations.C: A cat is not the required intermediate host for Hymenolepis diminuta; its cycle depends on an arthropod intermediate host instead.
explanations.D: A rat can be the definitive host of Hymenolepis diminuta (hence its common name, the rat tapeworm), but the egg itself must first be ingested by an arthropod intermediate host before the cycle can be completed, not directly by a rat.

questions.question: Most common intermediate host for Echinococcus granulosus is:

explanations.A: Man is only an accidental, occasional intermediate host for Echinococcus granulosus, not its most common one.
explanations.B: The dog is the definitive host of Echinococcus granulosus, harbouring the adult tapeworm in its intestine, not the intermediate host this question asks about.
explanations.C: The fox is a definitive host for some Echinococcus species (such as E. multilocularis) but is not the most common intermediate host for E. granulosus.

Recognising sheep as the commonest intermediate host, rather than man, dog or fox, is the fact tested here.

questions.question: Hydatid cyst is the larva of:

explanations.A: The hydatid cyst is the larva of Echinococcus granulosus, developing in the intermediate host (commonly sheep, occasionally man) after ingestion of eggs shed by an infected dog, the definitive host. questions.question: Cysticercosis occurs as a complication in infection with:

explanations.A: Cysticercosis occurs as a complication of infection with Taenia solium, through autoinfection in which the patient ingests their own eggs, allowing the larval cysticercus stage to develop within their own tissues, including muscle, subcutaneous tissue, the eye and the brain. This risk is specific to T. solium because man can act as both definitive host (harbouring the adult worm) and, through autoinfection, an accidental intermediate host developing cysticerci. Recognising T. solium, not T. saginata, as the species that produces this human-tissue cysticercosis is the fact tested here.
explanations.B: Taenia saginata does not cause cysticercosis in man; the human intestine is a dead end for its eggs, which can only develop into cysticerci after being ingested by cattle.
explanations.C: Since Taenia saginata does not share this cysticercosis risk, "both of the above" is incorrect; the risk is specific to Taenia solium.
explanations.D: Fasciolopsis buski is an intestinal trematode with no larval cysticercus stage and is not associated with cysticercosis.

questions.question: Appendicitis is considered a complication of infection with:
